```{=html}
What is sports? There are many definitions. In German (my native language) *Sport* is often used for any movement disciplines or physical exercise. In English *sports* can be differentiated from exercise and other forms of physical activity. Sports is used only for clearly structured, performance- and competition-oriented movement disciplins.
I tried to come up with my own definition for sports that I use througout my writings. It's a working definition and I hope to break it at one point through my writing process.
### Sports defined:
*Sports is an umbrella term for structured movement practices that value goal-oriented performance under explicit rules.*
The rules change over time but are definitive and binding for all parties. Common rules ensure the two most dominant moral <!--# moral cause fixed defined standpoint; or ethical as broader discussion?-->
```

standpoint of sports: fairness and equality <!--#(Sure? Doubleck Gleichberechtigung/Gleichheit/Chancengleicheit)-->. <!--# Rulesets get revised frequently. They can even get adpated during an event or game just to serve fairness. This makes sports a unique small-scaled experiment of culture. Some have argured that without sports, some of the moral positions could not be understood and expressed as well in other domains of social life. Other key elements of sports could be fun, entertainment, progress and transcendence, all of which can affect the rules and structures of the sports.  However, I really think these are secondary because these are embeded in other social and individual actions as well.
By defining endgoals or final performance criteria, sports allows for a comparison between participants and over time. The comparison is only possible through the embedding of the moral principles in the ruleset (even if changing rulesets sometimes deny the comparison over time).
To me, it is an open question, if training should be a part of the definition of sports. The current *Zeitgeist* emphasises improvements of personal performance over time by structured practice and preparation (physical, psychological and technological). The opposing force would be talent as the predictor of performance. Training and talent are the sports equivalent of *nurture vs. nature*. If one or the other is more important is a question of perspective. I personally think that focusing on training embodies the ideal of equality in sports but does so only under the assumption of free-will or personal autonomy. The story goes like this: If training is the more imporant factor, the person who is smarter, more dedicated, has more willpower, grit or passion wins. If talent is more important, the person with better genes wins. The latter, so the story, has accomplished nothing by themself, while the first is truelly self-made and actualized. I love the story and buy it on an emotional level. However, it only works out if you conflate every motivational and cognitive aspect with the Self and the body under the control of genes. If we break this up and realize that at least part of the "grit" and "willpower" must be hereted or tought in early childhood it's not so clear where to split this aspect of nurture and nature (as every other aspect of the pair).
